Let \(n=2p\). Since \(p\) is odd, none of the even indices \(2,4,\dots,2p-2\) equals \(p\). For \(1\le t\le 2p-1\), \(t\ne p\), Legendre’s formula gives
\[
v_p\binom{2p}{t}=1.
\]
So every \(\binom{2p}{2j}\) is divisible by exactly one factor of \(p\). Also
\[
\binom{2p}{2}=p(2p-1),
\]
so
\[
H_p=pD,\qquad D\mid 2p-1.
\]

Now let \(q\) be a prime divisor of \(2p-1\). Since \(q\ne p\), whether \(q\mid D\) is exactly whether
\[
q\mid \binom{2p}{2j}
\]
for every \(1\le j\le p-1\).

Write \(2p-1=m\), so \(2p=m+1\). We use Lucas’ theorem modulo \(q\): \(\binom{m+1}{t}\not\equiv0\pmod q\) iff every base-\(q\) digit of \(t\) is at most the corresponding digit of \(m+1\).

Because \(q\mid m\), the base-\(q\) expansion of \(m+1\) ends in digit \(1\). If \(m\) is not a power of \(q\), then \(m+1\ne 1+q^a\). Hence some even interior number \(t=1+q^r\), with \(2\le t\le m-1\), has base-\(q\) digits bounded by those of \(m+1\). Lucas then gives
\[
\binom{m+1}{t}\not\equiv0\pmod q,
\]
so \(q\nmid D\).

If instead \(m=q^a\), then \(m+1=q^a+1\). Its only nonzero base-\(q\) digits are the units digit and the \(q^a\)-digit. The only \(t\) with digitwise-bounded digits are
\[
0,\ 1,\ q^a,\ q^a+1.
\]
None is an even interior index. Thus every even interior binomial coefficient is divisible by \(q\), so \(q\mid D\).

Finally, no higher power \(q^2\) can divide all the reduced coefficients. If \(a=1\),
\[
\frac1p\binom{2p}{2}=q.
\]
If \(a\ge2\), take \(t=q^{a-1}+1\), which is even; Kummer’s theorem shows exactly one carry in adding \(t\) and \(q^a+1-t\), so
\[
v_q\binom{q^a+1}{q^{a-1}+1}=1.
\]
Thus only one factor of \(q\) is common.

Therefore
\[
\boxed{
H_p=
\begin{cases}
pq, & \text{if }2p-1=q^a\text{ for some prime }q\text{ and integer }a\ge1,\\
p, & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}}
\]
